results.content: # Thoracic: Education: Statistics for Surgeons Statistical power and sample size calculations for time-to-event analysis. To provide thoracic and cardiovascular surgeons with the necessary tools for performing sample size and power calculations for studies with time-to-event outcomes. Power and sample size calculations enhance the overall quality of research studies by providing readers with assurance and insight into the number of patients included in the study. A 5-step approach is presented for performing sample size calculations in comparing groups on time-to-event endpoints. Statistical power is an essential element for designing studies to ensure sufficient sample sizes for detecting treatment effects or group differences in time-to-event patient outcomes. Power and sample size justification not only adds statistical rigor and credibility to research manuscripts, but also provides the reader with assurance that the findings and conclusions are valid and based on a sufficient number of patients.

results.title: [PDF] Sample Size Calculations for Randomized Controlled Trials
results.content: Having introduced a basic formula for sample size, the review discusses each element of the formula in relation to its applicability to controlled trials and then points to special complexities faced by many controlled trials—how the use of multiple primary endpoints, multiple treatment arms, and sequential monitoring affects the type I error rate and hence how these considerations should influence the choice of sample size; how staggered entry and lag time to effect of therapy affect statistical power in studies with binary or time-to-failure endpoints; how noncompliance with pre-scribed therapy attenuates the difference between treated groups and control groups; and how to adjust sample size during the course of the trial to maintain desired power.

results.title: statistical power - How to calculate effect of sample size on false positive rate? - Cross Validated
results.content: # [How to calculate effect of sample size on false positive rate? [duplicate]](/questions/662600/how-to-calculate-effect-of-sample-size-on-false-positive-rate). Critics of the study state that smaller sample size increases false positive rate, even though P value is 0.04 (false positive rate of 4%). It is not exactly true that "a smaller sample size increases false positive rate" in the sense that you would be more likely to see e.g. ## Calculate a Chi-Square test P-value ## M is the number of successes (or failures) in each group ## N is the shared sample size for each group, i.e. the other row is N-M chisq <- \(M, N) { O <- M nO <- N-M E <- rowSums(M)/ncol(M) nE <- N-E Chi <- rowSums((O-E)^2/E) + rowSums((nO-nE)^2/nE) P <- pchisq(Chi, ncol(M)-1, lower.tail=FALSE) P[is.na(P)] <- 1 ## Degenerate when all rows zero -- this is never significant return(P) } ## Simulate a number of studies and do a Chi-Square test ## N is the (shared) sample size of each arm ## P0 and P1 are the control and test risks ## iters is the number of replicate studies simulate_chisq <- function(N, P0, P1=P0, iters=1E6) { M <- cbind(rbinom(iters, N, P1), rbinom(iters, N, P0)) probs <- chisq(M, N) return(probs) } set.seed(1) sims <- cbind( large <- simulate_chisq(N=1350, P0=0.10), medium <- simulate_chisq(N=500, P0=0.10), small <- simulate_chisq(N=150, P0=0.10) ) |> magrittr::set_colnames(c("large", "medium", "small")) colMeans(sims < 0.05) #> large medium small #> 0.049784 0.049481 0.049730. What *is* true is that smaller studies have a higher probability of giving estimated effect sizes that are further removed from the truth: for example, seeing a 3% difference in mortality when the true risk is 10% in both arms occurs with probability $\approx 0.263$ in a study of N=250 per arm, and only $\approx 0.063$ for N=675 per arm. The counterpoint here is that you shouldn't *overpower* your study either, because as sample size grows any infinitesimal difference can be made statistically significant. Now, the real kicker is in studies that were not properly powered to detect a meaningful effect: *if* you condition on such studies being significant, then their effect size estimates are likely to be inflated compared to the truth. Studies with small sample sizes.
